desc:
A string s consists of English letters in both lower and upper case. Whenever two neighbouring characters are the same letter in different cases (for example 'e' and 'E', in either order), you may delete both of them; the characters on their two sides then become neighbours. Keep doing this for as long as such a pair exists.

Return the string that remains. The result does not depend on which pair you delete first, and it may be empty.

Example: 'abBAcC' becomes 'aAcC' (delete bB), then 'cC' (delete aA), then the empty string. Another: 'leEeetcode' becomes 'leetcode', because 'ee' is not a pair (same case).
constraints: s consists of lowercase and uppercase English letters
The answer may be the empty string
hints: Deleting a pair can bring two characters together that were far apart in the input, so a single left-to-right look at neighbours is not enough.
The only character that a new character can ever cancel with is the last one that survived so far. Think of the survivors as a pile where only the top is reachable.

Keep a stack of survivors. For each character, if the stack is non-empty and the top is the same letter in the other case (top != ch and top.lower() == ch.lower()), pop; otherwise push. The stack read from bottom to top is the answer.
editorial: Scan the string from left to right and keep the surviving characters in a stack. A new character can only cancel with the character right before it in the current, already reduced text, and that is the top of the stack. If the two are the same letter in different cases, pop the top and discard the new character. Otherwise the new character stays and is pushed.

After a pop, the new top is exactly the character that became adjacent to the next input character, so chains such as 'abBA' collapse completely without any extra work. Every character is pushed and popped at most once, so the time is O(n) with O(n) space. The result is independent of the deletion order because the stack always produces the fully reduced string.
